disclaimer: Synthetic instructor-style documents for engineering evaluation only. Ten manually annotated one-relevant-passage questions; this is not an independent medical or clinical benchmark.

materials.text:
Cuff skills workshop

The MapleCuff classroom station uses three sequential seated blood-pressure readings after a quiet rest. In this fictional exercise, learners record the final reading in their practice worksheet.

The station also asks students to note the cuff size and the arm position.

Measurement units lecture

The BridgeGauge practice card asks learners to write pressure readings in millimetres of mercury, abbreviated mmHg. Its example uses two numbers separated by a slash.

This is a classroom notation exercise, not a patient diagnosis.

Respiratory symptom diary

The CedarDiary exercise asks learners to record a simulated pollen exposure alongside the date and any reported wheeze. The entries describe a fictional scenario, not a clinical finding.

The exercise distinguishes a potential trigger from a confirmed diagnosis.

Device demonstration

The HarborSpacer classroom demonstration uses an empty training inhaler and a demonstration spacer to practise device handling. No medication is administered in the classroom scenario.

The worksheet records the student demonstration steps.

Nutrition exercise

The OrchardPlate worksheet asks students to compare the carbohydrate information on two fictional meal labels. Learners record which label lists more carbohydrates per serving.

This is an educational calculation task rather than a treatment recommendation.

Graph interpretation exercise

The FinchGraph class example plots simulated glucose measurements against time on a labelled horizontal axis. Students identify the highest plotted value without diagnosing anyone.

The data is entirely synthetic.

Headache diary activity

The LanternLog simulated diary tracks the timing of bright-light exposure and headache descriptions across four invented school days. The class discusses the difference between a correlation and a proven cause.

The exercise is not a medical risk estimate.

Symptom categorization activity

The RiverCard exercise sorts fictional symptom cards into visual changes, sound sensitivity and other observations. Students explain why an observation alone is not a diagnosis.

These cards are for teaching only.

Fictional case-note practice

The MeadowCase worksheet places a mock symptom report before a fictional imaging note in a classroom timeline. Students identify the order in which information was recorded.

No actual patient data is included.

Source review workshop

The CompassSource exercise asks learners to check a source publication date before comparing two mock educational summaries about lung infection. Students label which summary was published more recently.

It is a provenance exercise, not clinical guidance.
